introduction: The museum exists because of one man's will. Ferenc Hopp, a Budapest optician who travelled widely in Asia, left his villa, garden and collection to the state in 1919 on condition that they become a museum bearing his name.
chapters: Ferenc Hopp was born in Fulnek in Moravia on 28 April 1833. Hungarian Wikipedia says he began as an optician's apprentice at the age of thirteen under István Calderoni, was sent to Vienna in 1853 and then to New York, returned in 1861 and took over the firm in 1864 while keeping its name. The firm made optical instruments and cameras and introduced the manufacture of school teaching aids to Hungary. Once he could afford to travel, he made five journeys around the world; sources date them slightly differently, but all place them between the early 1880s and the 1910s. East Asia, above all China and Japan, drew him most. Hungarian Wikipedia says he bought about 1,200 Chinese objects between 1883 and 1914, and his Japanese collection reached nearly 2,000 items by his death.

Hopp died in Budapest on 9 September 1919. In his will he left his villa and garden at Andrássy út 103 and his collection to the Hungarian state. Sources give the size of the collection as about 4,000 to more than 4,500 objects. He had first thought of dividing the collection among the Museum of Fine Arts, the Museum of Applied Arts and the Ethnographic Museum, but he decided instead on a single museum. His will required that the villa be used as an East Asian art museum and that the museum should always carry his name. It also required that other state-owned Eastern collections be added to his own.

The Ferenc Hopp Museum of Asiatic Arts opened in 1923, and Zoltán Felvinczi Takács, who described Hopp in 1914, became its first director. Objects were transferred from the Museum of Applied Arts, the Museum of Fine Arts, the Ethnographic Museum and the Hungarian National Museum, and private collections such as Vince Wartha's, Jenő Zichy's North Asian material and Imre Schwaiger's Indian collection were added. After 1945 the museum received state gifts from Vietnam, China and North Korea. Hungarian Wikipedia gives about 23,000 objects in 2006, and a 2021 article gives about 30,000. The villa garden still holds the statues, pagodas and memorial columns that Hopp put there.

introduction: The tower is the only part of the Church of Mary Magdalene still standing. The church served Buda's Hungarian community for centuries, passed through Ottoman, Franciscan and military hands, and was demolished after damage in the siege of 1944 to 1945.
chapters: A parish church for the Hungarians of Buda

According to the Castle District heritage site, the parish was formed in the middle of the thirteenth century, soon after the town's founding, as a chapel of the parish of the Matthias Church. Excavations show that the first church was small, with a single nave. By the end of the fifteenth century a late Gothic church had been completed with six vault sections, an enlarged chancel and a five-storey tower on its western front, built by the town's Hungarian community. A news article gives 1247 and King Béla IV as the origin, so the sources differ on the earliest date. Both agree that the church was the Hungarian counterpart of the Matthias Church, which served the German population.
Ottoman rule, Franciscans and the garrison

During the Ottoman era it was the only Christian church on the castle hill, shared by Catholics and Protestants. In the Fifteen Years War, from 1591 to 1606, the Christians lost the building and it became a Muslim place of worship. The siege of 1686 left the church badly damaged, and only the tower could still be used. The Franciscans then removed the Gothic remains and built a Baroque church and monastery, repairing the medieval tower in Baroque style. Joseph II closed the monastery. In 1792 Francis I was crowned king of Hungary in the church, and in 1817 it was given to the Buda garrison. In the late nineteenth century, while the Matthias Church was being rebuilt, the parish moved here. In 1920 it became the church of the Roman Catholic Military Bishopric.
Destruction in 1945 and the surviving tower

In the siege of 1944 and 1945 the vaults of the nave and sanctuary collapsed. Repairs began straight after the fighting, but full restoration never happened, and when the military bishopric ceased the church had no maintainer. Reconstruction of the tower began in 1950, and the church building was demolished at the same time. The former churchyard is now an archaeological park behind a glass wall, and the site of the nave is a garden of ruins. The tower was reported to have opened to tourists in 2017. A news article from March 2025 says the district council took back the operator's concession and closed the tower while it developed a new concept, so the tower's present status should be checked.
